title_en: Cliff Sosin - Owning the Complements to Intelligence - [Invest Like the Best, EP.497]
title_zh: Cliff Sosin：拥有智能的互补品——当智能变得廉价而无处不在（Invest Like the Best EP.497）
subtitle_zh: Cliff Sosin 论证智能有内在极限，数据、注意力与物理邻近才是廉价智能的真正互补品。
summary_zh: 本期 Invest Like the Best 中 Patrick O'Shaughnessy 与投资人 Cliff Sosin 展开一场关于「智能的未来及其对市场与公司意味」的思想对话，核心命题是「只是智能」（it's just intelligence）。Sosin 反驳「智能无上限、终将变成上帝」的观念：智能更像一个比率、像球的「圆度」，是我们在事实之间做插值的工具。数学这类问题可以解到完美，但世界上绝大多数有趣的问题属于复杂动力系统（complex dynamic system），像天气一样没有闭式解、模拟必然累积误差——他用混沌理论与「蝴蝶效应」的经典故事说明，即便完美的智能，其适用性仍然有限。要突破，就必须出去做实验、触碰现实、获取更多信息，而这需要时间。他进一步指出，智能施展之处恰恰是降低自身成本，「足够好」的智能价格正迅速下跌，终将近乎免费而无处不在。由此引出真正的投资命题：当智能变得廉价，其互补品（complements）——数据、注意力、物理邻近，以及协调二阶效应的能力——才是持久经济性所在。节目也谈及资本周期（capital cycles）、数据中心供给建设的狂热，以及「所有人都往同一条明显路径挤反而变坏」的反身性，提供了与主流「无限建设、需求无上限」叙事截然不同的一副视角。

turns.en: Visit workos.com to get started. You called me saying it's just intelligence was sort of the theme of our conversation. That simple idea. There's this idea that if intelligence starts in Amoeba and it gets better and better and then it's like a monkey and then it's like a person and then it's like Einstein and then it goes zoom and it becomes God.
turns.zh: 访问 workos.com 即可开始。你之前打电话跟我说，'只是智能（it's just intelligence）'差不多是我们这期对话的主题。就是那个简单的想法。有一种观念认为，智能从变形虫开始，越来越强，然后像猴子，然后像人，然后像爱因斯坦，再接着嗖的一下，变成了上帝。

turns.en: I think that that's something of an intellectual mistake. What people have wrong there is they're missing where the real limits of what intelligence can do.
turns.zh: 我认为那在某种程度上是一个智识错误。人们搞错的地方，是他们不理解智能真正能做到什么的边界在哪里。

turns.en: And maybe another way to put it, if you think about intelligence as like an unbounded scalar at the height of a tree, isn't correct. What you should really think about intelligence as is more like a ratio, like the roundness of a ball.
turns.zh: 或者换个说法，如果你把智能想象成树顶上的一把没有上限的标量，那是不对的。你真正应该把智能想象成更像是一个比率——就像一个球的圆度。

turns.en: And intelligence is a gadget and we use it to make predictions about the universe. And so we start with this thin scattering of facts about the universe where we have relatively few of them and the universe is complex.
turns.zh: 智能是一件工具（gadget），我们用它对宇宙做出预测。所以我们起步时，关于宇宙只有稀稀落落的一小撮事实，数量相当有限，而宇宙是复杂的。

turns.en: And we use intelligence to interpolate between them. So as your intelligence goes up, your ability to color in the spaces gets better. And some domains are really amenable to that in mathematics.
turns.zh: 我们用智能在事实之间做插值。所以你的智能越高，把空白处填色的能力就越强。有些领域特别适合这样做，比如数学。

turns.en: You can solve those sorts of things. And in those areas, you get to perfect. For most of the interesting stuff that is most of the questions in the world, the mathematical term is a complex dynamic system.
turns.zh: 这类问题你能解出来，在那些领域你可以做到完美。但对于世界上绝大多数有趣的事情——也就是绝大多数的问——数学术语叫复杂动力系统（complex dynamic system）。

turns.en: So what that basically means is they're kind of like weather in the sense that you can't just guess your way. You can't make a closed form answer.
turns.zh: 这基本上意味着，它们有点像天气：你没法靠猜得出答案，也写不出闭式解。

turns.en: You can try to simulate it, but if you simulate it invariably, your simulation will have some degree of error in your initial conditions or in each step going forward, because at a minimum, your steps, for example, are going to be truncated.
turns.zh: 你可以尝试模拟它，但只要去模拟，你的模拟就必然带有某种程度的误差——初始条件里有，往后每一步也会有——因为最起码，你的时间步长是被截断的。

turns.en: And so what happens is your error will build and invariably after the simulation runs for some period of time, you'll be off by some amount.
turns.zh: 于是误差会不断累积，模拟运行一段时间之后，你必然会出现某种程度的偏离。

turns.en: And so for mixing cream into your coffee or predicting the weather or thinking about how groups of people who are all very complicated are going to interact with each other, intelligence just isn't that powerful.
turns.zh: 所以，无论是把奶油搅进咖啡、预测天气，还是琢磨一群个个复杂的人将如何相互互动，智能就是没有那么强大。

turns.en: And so my sense is that what you get is this increasing intelligence to the point where you are making all the predictions as something that's super smart could make, which it turns out is a relatively small set of all the interesting things you'd want to know about the world.
turns.zh: 所以我的感觉是，智能不断提高，最终达到某个更聪明的存在所能做出的所有预测——而事实证明，那只是你想知道的关于这个世界所有有趣问题中相当小的一部分。

turns.en: To get past that, you then need to go out and get more information about the world, and that just takes time. You have to do experiments, you have to touch reality.
turns.zh: 要突破这一点，你就必须出去获取更多关于世界的信息，而这就需要时间。你必须做实验，你必须触碰现实。

turns.en: One interesting corollary to that is that the zoom actually becomes one of the things you can turn your intelligence to is reducing the cost of intelligence, which we're seeing.
turns.zh: 一个有趣的问题是：智能本身能施展的地方之一，恰恰是降低智能的成本——而这是我们正在看到的。

turns.en: So what you actually end up getting is everyone gets unlimited, really great, very round ball, so to speak, intelligence for essentially free.
turns.zh: 所以你最终得到的，是每个人本质上都能免费获得无限的、非常好的、非常圆的球——也就是智能。

turns.en: And obviously that's a limit statement, it won't actually be free. But the point is that what we're seeing is that really good enough intelligence is rapidly falling in price.
turns.zh: 显然这是个极限说法，它不会真的免费。但要点是，我们正看到足够好的智能的价格在迅速下跌。

turns.en: It turns out that really good enough intelligence will solve the vast majority of questions where people need to use intelligence. Yeah, can you say more about why this notion of a complex adaptive or dynamic system means that actually even perfect intelligence or whatever intelligence we have in a bottle ten years from now or pick your horizon will still be limited in its applications?
turns.zh: 事实证明，足够好的智能就能解决人们需要动用智能的绝大多数问题。嗯，你能不能多讲讲，为什么复杂自适应或复杂动力系统这个概念意味着，实际上即便是完美的智能——或者十年之后装在瓶子里的智能，你爱选什么期限选什么期限——在适用性上仍然有限？

turns.en: Yes, nonlinear dynamic systems. The famous story here and how these were discovered is came into the branch of mathematics that became chaos theory is back in the day, there was a guy who was building a weather forecast testing model back on big computers that took up rooms and that sort of thing.
turns.zh: 可以。非线性动力系统。这里有个著名的故事，也是这门学问如何被发现的：它进入数学的分支后来成了混沌理论。当年有个人在一台占满整个房间的大计算机上搭建天气预测模型。

turns.en: So he runs the model and it makes predictions of pressure and temperature over some span of some forecasting period and he's like, cool. And so then just to make sure it's still working, they reset it and they run it again.
turns.zh: 他运行模型，模型在某个预测时段内给出气压和温度的预测，他觉得挺好。然后为了确认程序还在正常工作，他把初始条件重置，再跑一遍。

turns.en: And it starts out basically the same results, but then the results start to diverge and by the third, fourth, fifth day of the forecast, the results were entirely different.
turns.zh: 结果一开始基本一样，但随后结果开始发散，到了预报的第三、四、五天，结果已经完全不同。

turns.en: And the guy thought some version of darn, I must have a bug in my system and begins in the process of trying to figure out why the computer isn't producing the same results in repeated runs.
turns.zh: 这人心里大概是想：该死，我系统里肯定有 bug，于是开始排查为什么计算机重复运行给不出相同的结果。

turns.en: And it turned out that the technician who had loaded the data into the computer in the second run had rounded off at some decimal, like one decimal less, all of the initial conditions for pressure and temperature and such.
turns.zh: 结果发现，是那位第二次把数据录入电脑的技师，在所有初始气压、温度等条件上少保留了一位小数。

turns.en: And you would have thought that, okay, maybe that would have produced a small but consistent error over the whole forecast period. But what had actually happened was that small error through all of the repeated steps, you take your current conditions, you calculate your next set of conditions, they compound and you had an entirely different forecast by some small distance into the forecasting period and the unrecognizable weather.
turns.zh: 你本来会觉得，好吧，也许那会在整个预测期内造成一个微小但一致的误差。但实际发生的是，那个小误差经过反复的每一步迭代——你拿当前条件算下一组条件——不断复利放大，仅仅几天之后预报就面目全非，天气完全认不出来了。

turns.en: One model said it was 70 degrees and sunny and the other model said it was 20 degrees and pouring. People called it the butterfly effect because at least in principle, butterfly could flap its wings in Africa and that could lead to a hurricane in North America and whatnot.
turns.zh: 一个模型说华氏 70 度、晴空万里，另一个模型说华氏 20 度、暴雨倾盆。人们把它叫作蝴蝶效应——至少原则上，一只蝴蝶在非洲扇动翅膀，就可能给北美带来一场飓风，云云。

turns.en: And it just turns out that many systems that we're interested in have this characteristic. You can know everything about pressure and temperature, but you can't necessarily write down an equation that you can solve easily that would tell you that there's going to be a hurricane.
turns.zh: 结果证明，我们感兴趣的许多系统都有这种特性。你可以对气压和温度了如指掌，却未必能写出一套容易求解的方程来告诉你飓风要来了。

turns.en: You have to model it. And the model in turn is going to be greened at some level unless you actually go to the step of actually having the whole universe.
turns.zh: 你必须去建模。而模型本身在某个尺度上必然是有颗粒度的——除非你真的走到拥有整个宇宙这一步。

turns.en: And so ultimately in the limit, if you want to simulate the whole universe, what you actually need is the whole universe. If you don't actually do that, there are many, many circumstances where simulation is super useful for approximations and in those circumstances, you can use intelligence to solve them, but there are many more where it doesn't work.
turns.zh: 所以最终在极限意义上，要想模拟整个宇宙，你需要的就是整个宇宙。不这么做的话，仍有大量情形里模拟作为近似极其有用，那些情形你可以用智能来解决，但更多的情形是行不通的。

turns.en: And so intelligence is limited in that fundamental unknowableness, I guess, about the universe. So back to this notion of it's just intelligence.
turns.zh: 所以智能受制于那种宇宙根本上的不可知性。我想就是这样。回到'只是智能'这个说法。

turns.en: What does that mean about where you think we're going from a more practical standpoint? We're all going to have a team of 200 IQ people working full time in our pocket and that team will have a team that it can deploy of many more.
turns.zh: 从更实际的角度看，这意味着我们要走向哪里？我们都会有一支 200 智商的团队全天候装在口袋里工作，而这个团队还能再派出更多这样的团队。

turns.en: And they're going to be trying to figure out all the little optimizations that were too lazy to do. And every company will make similar teams available to their employees in order to do their jobs.
turns.zh: 他们会帮你把过去你懒得做的那些小优化全搞定。每家公司都会给员工提供类似的团队，好让他们完成工作。

turns.en: There's just a lot of businesses where that's not good for them. Consumers are boundedly rational at present. They only have so much cognitive space.
turns.zh: 有很多生意这么做对它们并不利。消费者目前是有限理性的，他们的认知带宽只有那么多。

turns.en: And so you go to a consumer and you say, look, we'll take your money, we won't steal it, we'll pay you a decent interest rate, you don't have to think about it, and you can go about your life.
turns.zh: 所以你去找一个消费者说：听着，我们收你的钱，不偷你的钱，给你付个体面的利率，你不用操心，继续过你的日子。

turns.en: And the consumer doesn't say, look, if I think about this every day, I could say, $400 a year, so therefore I'm going to think about this every day.
turns.zh: 消费者不会说：如果我每天琢磨这件事，我能一年多出 400 美元，所以我决定每天都来琢磨它。

turns.en: The consumer says something like, eh, sounds good enough, and I'm going to move on. But with an agent, you would think the agent will continuously optimize for them.
turns.zh: 消费者会说：呃，听起来够好了，我继续过日子去。但换成智能体，你可能会觉得智能体会一直替他们优化。

turns.en: Then there's also companies where what they produce fundamentally is some sort of artifact that is just some sort of crystallized intelligence.
turns.zh: 还有一类公司，它们生产的东西本质上就是某种结晶化的智能（crystallized intelligence）的制品。

turns.en: And by far not the first person to realize that AI could be bad for certain software companies, but just this idea that what an AI model is, is it's kind of like this general purpose intelligence tool.
turns.zh: 意识到 AI 可能对某些软件公司不利的人远不止我一个，但就是这个想法：AI 模型本质上是一个通用的智能工具。

turns.en: And what many software tools are, are crystallized and hardened pieces, like projections of intelligence. And so as I've been thinking about companies and investments, I found it helpful to assume everyone has really great intelligence and ask what's left.
turns.zh: 而许多软件工具，是结晶化、固化的一块块智能投影。所以在思考公司和投资时，我发现有一个思路很有帮助：假设人人都有非常好的智能，然后问还剩下什么。

turns.en: The pushback is often some version of, but you don't understand how hard this is, and you don't understand how complicated this is, and you don't understand how many smart people have had to think for so long about this, and my hand wavy and approximately right response is, okay, sure, but that's all just intelligence.
turns.zh: 常见的反驳通常是某种版本的：你不懂这有多难，你不懂这有多复杂，你不懂有多少人得琢磨这么久。而我那个含糊但大致正确的回应是：好吧，没错，但那些统统只是智能。

turns.en: And to follow this logic all the way through to the end is, if intelligence becomes cheap and ubiquitous, what you want to own are the compliments to intelligence, and so the compliments to intelligence are their data, attention, love, affection, whatever sort of emotional attachment you want.
turns.zh: 把这个逻辑一路推演到底就是：如果智能变得廉价而无处不在，你想拥有的就是智能的互补品（complements）。而智能的互补品是数据、注意力、爱、情感——任何你想要的情感依附。

turns.en: It's physical proximity, it's scale, it's a little cynical, but it's regulatory capture. It's these sorts of things where for some businesses, what happens is their finite ability to deploy intelligence, be it economics, just the cost of it, they're only a certain size company and they don't have access to 10,000 of Google's best engineers for 10 years, or be it just that the organization is behind or whatever, the ability to deploy way more
turns.zh: 还有物理邻近性、规模；有点愤世嫉俗地说，还有监管俘获（regulatory capture）。就是这类东西。对某些企业来说，发生的是：它们部署智能的能力是有限的——可能是经济上的，就是成本，它们只是那么大一家公司，请不到 Google 的一万名顶尖工程师干上十年；也可能是组织落后之类——把更多智能部署进你生意的能力、

turns.en: intelligence to your business, and your competitors to deploy more intelligence to their business, and your customers to use lots of intelligence, it can work out to be better for you, or if intelligence is a barrier to you serving your customers, the lack of it, or it can be bad for you if your customer's lethargy is the fundamental element of your economic value.
turns.zh: 你的竞争对手把更多智能部署进他们的生意、你的客户使用大量智能，最终可能对你更有利；或者，如果智能的缺乏是你服务客户的障碍，那智能变多对你有利；而如果客户惰性是你经济价值的根本要素，那它也可能对你不利。

turns.en: Maybe pick Metta or something as the perfect example of a company that I think you believe owns perfect compliments to ubiquitous cheap intelligence, just to bring the example to life.
turns.zh: 拿 Meta 或者别的什么公司举一个完美的例子吧——你觉得它拥有对无处不在的廉价智能的完美互补品——让例子生动一点。

turns.en: I'm actually going to set aside for a moment Muse and Agents and that whole thing and focus on business, and the core business at Metta is personalized TV.
turns.zh: 我其实打算先把 Muse、Agents 和那一整套东西放一放，聚焦于生意本身。Meta 的核心业务是个性化电视（personalized TV）。

turns.en: Personalized TV. It used to be social media, but now it's personalized TV, and it turns out that people really like watching Instagram or whatnot, discovered that I love dark British humor and it's great.
turns.zh: 个性化电视。它过去是社交媒体，但现在是个性化电视。结果发现人们真的很爱刷 Instagram 之类，还发现我自己很喜欢阴暗的英式幽默，感觉很棒。

turns.en: People talk about the 10,000 footer, let's talk about Metta from space, the highest view. They have 250 billion of revenue, and they spend $250 billion a year.
turns.zh: 人们爱说从一万英尺高空看问题，那我们从太空看 Meta，从最高处俯瞰。他们有 2500 亿美元的营收，而且一年花掉 2500 亿美元。

turns.en: Some of it gets accounted as first cost, some of it gets accounted for as capexed, it doesn't really matter, just they spend it all. The question you might ask is, what do they spend it on?
turns.zh: 有些记作营业成本，有些记作资本开支，无所谓，反正他们全花掉了。你可以问的问题是：他们花到哪儿去了？

turns.en: And a really reductionist view is that they spend it all on intelligence. What do I mean by that? Well, they're buying data centers. What is a data center?
turns.zh: 一个非常还原论的看法是，他们全花在智能上。我什么意思？他们在买数据中心。数据中心是什么？

turns.en: Well, it's kind of an intelligent producing tool. What else are they doing? Well, they're actually literally buying inference. That's just intelligence.
turns.zh: 某种程度上就是生产智能的工具。还在干嘛？他们其实在字面意义上直接购买推理（inference）——那就是智能。

turns.en: What else are they doing? They're buying really smart people to write algorithms, that's intelligence. They're writing code, also intelligence.
turns.zh: 还在干嘛？他们在雇非常聪明的人写算法——那是智能。他们在写代码——也是智能。

turns.en: They're surveying videos, that's intelligence adjacent, sure, intelligence. And so in some highly reductionist sense, and you shouldn't take these things literally, but I'm just trying to highlight the really big directions here.
turns.zh: 他们在审看视频——那是擦边智能，行吧，智能。所以在某种高度还原论的意义上——你不必把这些话当字面意思，我只是想凸显真正大的方向——

turns.en: All they buy is intelligence. And if you think forward with the fact that the price of intelligence is falling by a factor of 100 or something over the next five years, first principles, their costs kind of go away.
turns.zh: 他们买的一切都是智能。如果你沿着智能的价格在未来五年下降约 100 倍这个事实往前推，从第一性原理看，他们的成本就基本消失了。

turns.en: That's just thinking about the cost side of things. On the revenue side of things, there are all of the creators. You are a creator. How much more quality creative can every creator that makes content for Meta make?
turns.zh: 这只是成本面。收入面有所有的创作者。你就是创作者。每一个为 Meta 做内容的创作者，能多出多少优质创意？

turns.en: If they have access to intelligence, that's 100th the cost and 10,000 times more effective. The point is probably better. And then Meta, in turn, maybe they don't take their costs to zero.
turns.zh: 如果他们用上的智能成本低到百分之一、效能高出一万倍——结论大概是会更好。然后 Meta 自己，也许并不会把成本降到零。

turns.en: Maybe they spend more or more than zero and they do a far better job of picking the videos to show people next, which should make the content better targeted and more enjoyable.
turns.zh: 也许他们会花比零更多的钱，把下一步该给人们推什么视频挑得好得多，这会让内容更有针对性、更令人愉快。

turns.en: And then, of course, on the ad side, advertisers could make far better designed, far better targeted, personalized ads that then Meta, in turn, can target much better.
turns.zh: 然后当然在广告端，广告主可以设计出更好、投放更精准、个性化的广告，进而 Meta 又能把这些广告投放得更精准。

turns.en: And advertisers can also build much more slippery funnels or whatever to convert. The whole point of all this is that maybe instead of taking their costs to zero with much better intelligence and much lower prices, maybe they can sell a few more ads.
turns.zh: 广告主还能打造转化率高得多的漏斗之类。这一切的要点是：与其用更好更廉价的智能把成本降到零，不如多卖几条广告。

turns.en: All of this is downstream of what they possess, which is not destroyed by ubiquitous intelligence, which is data and attention. They just have this enormous amount of data about all these people and how they view videos and whatnot, and they have an enormous amount of attention and these things compound each other.
turns.zh: 所有这一切都源自他们所拥有的、不会被无处不在的智能摧毁的东西——数据和注意力。他们拥有海量的用户数据，记录着人们怎么看视频等等；他们还拥有海量的注意力，而这两者会相互放大。

turns.en: And so I don't think that the availability of cheap and ubiquitous intelligence is going to cause people not to be interested in watching funny 20-second videos.
turns.zh: 所以我不认为廉价而无处不在的智能，会导致人们不再对看 20 秒的搞笑视频感兴趣。

turns.en: And so if anything, they can win some time on the margin from other things people do at their time. I don't actually own it, but a company that benefits, in theory, from having a lot more intelligence is Grindr.
turns.zh: 所以如果他们能在边际上从人们手里多抢一点时间。我其实并不持有它的股票，但理论上会从多得多的智能中受益的一家公司是 Grindr。

turns.en: Basically, Grindr is the gate dating app, but it has been constrained over its life by the fact that it's just not that big of a company. And it turns out they've got lots of attention and they've got lots of data, but their ability to build all the things that you could imagine building on what ultimately amounts to a finite size team and budget and ability to create things has meant in some ways that Grindr
turns.zh: 基本上，Grindr 是同志交友软件，但它这辈子一直被一个事实限制着：它只是一家不大的公司。结果发现它有大量注意力、大量数据，但他们能在那支说到底是有限规模的团队、预算和创造力之上搭建一切的能力，意味着在某种意义上 Grindr

turns.en: can't be all the things you could imagine it could be. And again, I don't actually own any Grindr. I study lots of companies and that just sort of occurred to me.
turns.zh: 无法成为你能想象它成为的一切。再说一遍，我其实不持有 Grindr。我研究很多公司，这只是我突然想到的。

turns.en: This is another example of something where here, this mental model is, what if you had 10,000 of Google's best engineers to go work on your problem for five years?
turns.zh: 这是另一个例子：这个心智模型是——如果你有 Google 最好的 10000 名工程师去花五年解决你的问题，那会怎样？

turns.en: What could you do? And Grindr is one where maybe they could do more. I want to talk about the labs. So back to the original point, I think lots of great investors would say intelligence, specifically frontier intelligence is not a commodity.
turns.zh: 你能做成什么？Grindr 就是那种也许能做更多的公司。我想聊聊实验室（labs）。回到最初那点，我想很多优秀投资人会说，智能——特别是前沿智能——不是大宗商品。

turns.en: Historically, the conversation has been about the gap in intelligence between closed source and open source. Increasingly, the conversation is about the gap between what's publicly available from the labs and what's privately used by them inside their own businesses.
turns.zh: 历史上的讨论一直是闭源与开源之间的智能差距。如今的讨论越来越多地聚焦于实验室公开提供的能力、与他们内部业务自己使用的能力之间的差距。

turns.en: They seem to have figured out how to stop or slow distillation. Lots of people would say that there's this escape velocity thing happening and that the frontier token is going to be way more valuable and useful and that the labs themselves can then distill their own models and provide the best version of the cheap intelligence too.
turns.zh: 他们似乎已经找到了阻止或放缓蒸馏（distillation）的办法。很多人会说出现了某种逃逸速度（escape velocity）现象，前沿 token 会远远更有价值、更有用，实验室自己还能蒸馏自家模型，把廉价智能的最好版本也提供给市场。

turns.en: I'm curious for you to riff on the labs as companies through this mind of an investor. If they have models that are better and the ability to produce adequate intelligence at way lower cost than everybody else and nobody can copy it, then it's going to be a great business.
turns.zh: 很好奇你以一个投资者的心智来聊聊实验室作为公司这件事。如果他们拥有更好的模型、能以远低于他人的成本生产足够的智能、而没人能复制，那将是一门很棒的生意。

turns.en: I guess I have a couple of thoughts. As I've watched models get deployed, it feels like one way to think about it is you start out with these very inadequate models that are basically able to do a very small subset of jobs.
turns.zh: 我想有两三点看法。看着模型被部署落地，一个理解方式是：你起步时得到的是一些很不完善的模型，基本上只能做一小部分工作。

turns.en: What happens is the models get better and they work through and up the stack. With each successive step up, the frontier model has unlocked a larger, call it addressable market.
turns.zh: 接下来发生的是模型变好，一层层向上打通栈。每向上一步，前沿模型就解锁一个更大的、姑且称为可触达的市场。

turns.en: But behind it, what's happening is that once eVolver gets saturated, you would never use a frontier model for a chatbot in a customer service application.
turns.zh: 但在它身后，正在发生的是：一旦某个领域饱和——比如你永远不会用前沿模型去做客服应用里的聊天机器人。

turns.en: You'd be an idiot. What's happening is those areas, they clearly commoditize. There's this wave of hard tasks where you really need a frontier model and then behind that you don't.
turns.zh: 那你就是傻子。正在发生的是，那些领域显然会商品化。会有一波硬任务浪潮真正需要前沿模型，但在它身后就不需要了。

turns.en: The friends I have who are big frontier labs, companies, bulls or whatever, and obviously these companies are financials aren't public and they might have an information advantage over me, but would say something like, don't worry, we can also, along the whole efficient frontier, produce cheaper tokens.
turns.zh: 我那些是大型前沿实验室、看多这些公司之类的朋友们——显然这些公司的财务不是公开的，他们可能对我有信息优势——会说类似：别担心，沿着整个有效前沿，我们也能生产更便宜的 token。

turns.en: Maybe they can right now. Maybe they can't right now. Maybe they will in a few years. Maybe they won't. It's been very hard to think about, certainly the trend has been rapid commoditization of these things.
turns.zh: 也许现在能，也许现在不能；也许几年后能，也许不能。这件事一直非常难判断，当然，趋势是这些东西的快速商品化。

turns.en: If you were to look at the rise of Chinese models in every step and at a minimum, the cost has been collapsing. Even if they do have a position where the tokens necessary to do tasks that are well behind the frontier, it might not be a very big market because it just doesn't cost that much in the scheme of things to deliver and it is competitive even if they are a cost leader in the shrinking commodity market.
turns.zh: 如果你看看中国模型的崛起，每一步至少成本都在坍塌。即便他们确实占据了一个位置，能做那些远在前沿之后的任务所需的 token，那个市场可能也不大，因为按整体格局来算，那些任务花不了多少钱；而且竞争激烈——即便他们是这个不断缩小的商品市场里的成本领先者。

turns.en: The other thing is that I think that programming was this huge use of models. As you push forward, the question becomes, for the next, next, next layers of intelligence, do you still have bigger and bigger places to go after?
turns.zh: 另一点是，我认为编程曾是模型的一个巨大用途。当你不断向前推进，问题就变成了：接下来一层又一层的智能，你还有越来越大的一块块市场可以去开拓吗？

turns.en: The bull story would be some version of, yes, people will pay anything for a model that can figure out how to cure cancer. Maybe that's true, but to go to our prior conversation, I think figuring out how to cure cancer requires touching reality and I'm not sure that more IQ gets you that.
turns.zh: 看多的故事会是某种版本的：是的，人们愿意为能找到治愈癌症方法的模型付出任何代价。也许这是真的，但回到我们之前的对话，我觉得弄清如何治愈癌症需要触碰现实，而我不确定更多的 IQ 就能做到。

turns.en: If you don't believe that there's some super incredible use cases where you can just chart an enormous amount of more intelligence, then you start getting this point where the next step up in terms of you're coding and then maybe something else, but you're getting the smaller niches.
turns.zh: 如果你不相信存在某些超乎想象的用例、仅仅靠堆更多智能就能开辟出来，那你就会开始走到这样一步：你在写代码，接下来也许是别的什么，但你会进入越来越小的利基。

turns.en: It's like this diamond shaped demand frontier where initially you get wider and wider uses and then actually it starts to get more and more rarefied.
turns.zh: 就像一个菱形的需求前沿（diamond-shaped demand frontier）：起初你的用途越来越宽，然后实际上开始变得越来越稀薄。

turns.en: How often do you really need a 300 IQ? One might start to ask and look, we're going to find out and I don't want to be too dogmatic, but it strikes me as totally reasonable that what we end up with is some version of there are very few use cases for super elite intelligence.
turns.zh: 你究竟多久才真正需要一个 300 的 IQ？人们可以开始这样问。你看，我们会有答案的，我不想太武断，但在我看来完全合理的是：我们最终会到达某种局面——超高精英智能的用例非常少。

turns.en: There are lots of use cases for very good intelligence. That very good intelligence is highly competitive and commoditized and if these frontier labs can somehow become cost leaders in doing that, there's a margin to make in being a cost leader, but then there's also just rampant deflation and then this question becomes like how big is the market if good enough intelligence is very, very cheap, then how much good enough
turns.zh: 非常好的智能的用例非常多；这种非常好的智能高度竞争激烈、被商品化。如果这些前沿实验室有办法成为这个市场的成本领先者，做成本领先者是有利润可赚的，但同时也会有猖獗的通缩，然后问题就变成：如果足够好的智能非常非常便宜，市场到底有多大？人们到底会买多少足够好的

turns.en: intelligence are people going to buy? I'll just keep playing the devil's advocate. The two things people might say in this case are Jevon's paradox that gets cheaper.
turns.zh: 智能？我继续扮演一下魔鬼代言人。这种情况下人们可能说的两点，其一是杰文斯悖论（Jevons paradox）：越便宜，

turns.en: We're just going to want to use more of it. I'm curious what you think about that. The second would be historically the new uses of intelligence have typically been discovered by highly intelligent people.
turns.zh: 我们就是想用得越多。很好奇你怎么看。其二是，历史上智能的新用途通常是由高智能的人发现的。

turns.en: My good friend says intelligence creates its own demand. What about that? What about the fact that maybe it's diamond shaped for humans if humans are driving the new questions that the intelligence is set after to answer, but what if the thing itself is creating the new questions and we train it to do that really effectively and just explore in an open-ended way in the way that all of humanity would be doing led by the
turns.zh: 我的一位好朋友说，智能会创造自己的需求。这话怎么说？还有，如果对人类来说是菱形的呢——如果是人类在驱动智能去回答新问题——但如果问题本身是由这个系统自己在创造，我们训练它非常有效地这样做，像过去全人类由 150+

turns.en: people with 150 plus IQ or something historically. Jevon's paradox is just a narrow example of price elasticity of demand. In general, all markets are U-shaped, so initially when the product is terrible, there's no demand and then the product gets better and people will pay a lot, but they won't buy very much and then as the price goes down, the size of the market will rise because it becomes Jevon's paradox essentially, but then you get to a point where further price decreases
turns.zh: IQ 以上的人引领的那样，以开放探索的方式去追问，那会怎样？杰文斯悖论只是需求价格弹性的一个狭窄例子。一般来说，所有市场都是 U 形的：起初产品很差，没有需求；然后产品变好，人们愿意付很多钱，但买得不多；接着随着价格下降，市场规模会上升，因为这本质上就是杰文斯悖论；但再往后，进一步降价

turns.en: don't actually drive enough demand and the market shrinks and eventually, of course, you take the price to zero, then the size of the market goes to zero.
turns.zh: 带不动足够多的需求，市场就会缩小；当然，最终你把价格降到零，市场规模也就归零了。

turns.en: One example that I've thought about is the cost of fiber optic communication or just communication. The cost of moving information used to be super high and people moved very little of it and then through a whole series of innovations, the cost of moving information went down a lot and the amount of information moved went up a ton and the market grew a lot for a long time and then the market stopped growing and the cost of moving information kept falling
turns.zh: 我思考过的一个例子是光纤通信——或者说就是通信——的成本。传输信息的成本曾经极高，人们传输的信息很少；然后经过一连串创新，传输信息的成本大幅下降，传输的信息量暴增，市场增长了很久；然后市场停止增长，而传输信息的成本还在继续下降，

turns.en: and the market kept shrinking and nowadays, cogent communications, I think, routes 30 or 40% of all IP traffic across the internet and it's through one of its divisions, which is not even its biggest division and cogent communications is a few billion dollar market cap company.
turns.zh: 市场却在继续缩小。如今，Cogent Communications 我猜路由了全互联网 30% 到 40% 的 IP 流量，还是通过它旗下一个甚至不是最大部门的事业部做的，而 Cogent Communications 只是一家几十亿美元市值的公司。

turns.en: It's just not a very big industry. Now, I'm not saying that we're going to get quite that small in terms of intelligence but Jevon's paradox is a statement about a particular spot on a curve which doesn't necessarily have to be true and as your other question about can more intelligence create more desire for intelligence, I mean, I have a couple of thoughts on that.
turns.zh: 这个行业就是不大。我不是说智能最后会缩到那么小，但杰文斯悖论说的是曲线上某一个特定位置，未必总成立。至于你的另一个问题——更多智能能否创造对智能更多的需求——我在这上面也有几点想法。

turns.en: Certainly maybe I started out by saying you need to touch reality to answer questions and so if you had a model and it was going to think more about physics, it could certainly think lots of interesting thoughts about physics, but eventually it's going to need to do experiments and that's not to say we couldn't also do experiments but now we're bound by our ability to physically do experiments and so I think there's going to be this incredible time where
turns.zh: 当然，也许。我开头说过，回答问题需要触碰现实。所以如果你有一个模型，让它更多地思考物理，它当然能想出很多有趣的物理念头，但最终它需要去做实验。这并非说我们不能去做实验，但现在我们受制于物理上做实验的能力。所以我认为会有一段不可思议的时期：

turns.en: there's going to be so many cool discoveries which we already started to read about where this paper was written and this paper was written and this paper was written and if somebody had read all three papers and thought about it, they would have realized this but nobody had but it turns out the models read all the papers and they'll have to figure that out.
turns.zh: 会出现很多很酷的发现。我们已经开始看到这类报道——这篇论文写了，那篇论文写了，第三篇论文也写了，如果有人读过这三篇并加以思考，本该意识到这一点，但没人做到——结果模型读完了所有论文，把它们串了起来。

turns.en: There's going to be all kinds of great stuff that falls out of that but at some point we're going to kind of finish that and then it's going to be about like, hey, there's some way to think about things that are outside of what we know and we have a hypothesis but a model, even a super smart model, won't be better at guessing that necessarily, will be better at guessing that than the smartest person but the smartest person's odds are
turns.zh: 由此会涌现各种各样的好东西，但到了某个点我们基本上会把这一波做完，然后问题就变成：嘿，有些东西在我们已知之外，我们有个假设，但一个模型——哪怕超聪明的模型——在这方面未必必然猜得更好。它会比最聪明的人猜得好，但最聪明的人猜中的概率

turns.en: super low anyway so it'll be able to come with great ideas for experiments to do and they'll be worth doing but that will limit our ability to expand.
turns.zh: 本来也极低。所以它能想出很值得做的实验点子，那些实验值得做，但这会限制我们向外扩张的能力。

turns.en: The other thing I just think about is my own use of AI on a lot of levels. One just to go back to the commodization thing, I've totally commoditized my use of models for it's worth, it's because I'm lazy about how I do a lot of my building for stuff.
turns.zh: 我思考的另一件事是我自己对 AI 的使用，在很多层面上。单说回到商品化这件事，我用模型的方式已经完全商品化了，原因是我在构建东西上很懒。

turns.en: I'll tell a Grockbot to build things and because I don't want to use up all my Grockbot weed tokens, I then have it run all of them, I subscribe to all the things and I'll have it build using those subscriptions on a server and so I actually don't know what model I'm using anymore.
turns.zh: 我会叫 Grok bot 去建东西，因为我不想把我的 Grok bot 的额度用完，我就让它自己把所有订阅都跑上——我订阅了所有服务——让它在我的服务器上利用这些订阅去构建，所以我其实已经不知道自己在用哪个模型了。

turns.en: I used to know this model's better, this one's worse, I no longer know. All of this is being optimized on the back end for me and all I know is that stuff is getting built and it's not using up my subscriptions and so we're good.
turns.zh: 我以前还知道这个模型更好、那个更差，现在我不知道了。这一切都在后台替我优化，我唯一知道的是东西在被建出来，而且没耗用我的订阅，所以我们很好。

turns.en: Ridgeline is the first end-to-end system of record with embedded AI for investment management firms running portfolio accounting, reconciliation, reporting, trading, and compliance on one unified platform.
turns.zh: Ridgeline 是第一个端到端、内嵌 AI 的记录系统（system of record），为投资管理公司提供投资组合会计、对账、报告、交易和合规，全部在一个统一平台上。

turns.en: Firms are moving off legacy technology and on to Ridgeline because of how far ahead Ridgeline's AI features are compared to anything else in investment management software.
turns.zh: 各家公司正在告别遗留技术、转向 Ridgeline，因为与投资管理软件里的任何其他产品相比，Ridgeline 的 AI 功能领先得多。

turns.en: I've been hearing from a lot of investment managers about AI and they fall roughly into two camps with some unsure where to even start and others convinced that they can build their own order management system over a weekend.
turns.zh: 我最近听到很多投资管理人谈 AI，他们大致分成两派：一派完全不知从哪里入手，另一派坚信自己一个周末就能搭出一套订单管理系统。

turns.en: The reality is that running an investment firm will always require governance, controls, and a single source of truth for your data and no amount of AI enthusiasm changes that requirement.
turns.zh: 现实是，经营一家投资公司永远需要治理、控制和数据的单一事实来源，再多 AI 热情也改变不了这个要求。

turns.en: Ridgeline is built on exactly that foundation which is why I believe that the firms that come out ahead in the AI era will be the ones running on Ridgeline's unified platform.
turns.zh: Ridgeline 正是建立在这个基础之上，所以我相信，在 AI 时代胜出的公司，会是那些运行在 Ridgeline 统一平台上的公司。

turns.en: If you're serious about your firm's AI strategy, Ridgeline should be part of that conversation and you can request a demo at ridgeline.ai. There's this batch of companies that I'm curious what you think about which is effectively real world experimentation companies that create a loop that's automatic.
turns.zh: 如果你认真看待公司的 AI 战略，Ridgeline 应该成为这场对话的一部分。访问 ridgeline.ai 即可预约演示。有一批公司我很好奇你怎么看，它们本质上是现实世界实验公司——搭建一个自动化的循环。

turns.en: There's this happening in robotics, there's this happening in several places in bio labs and automated wet labs, automated testing labs. Any commentary on that land of company?
turns.zh: 机器人领域有这种玩法，生物实验室自动湿实验室、自动测试实验室等好几个地方也有这种玩法。对这一类公司有什么评论吗？

turns.en: Yeah, super great idea. Using the loop in the physical world is going to be great and it's going to accelerate the process of learning and this is a great idea, but again, there are speed limits.
turns.zh: 是的，非常棒的主意。在物理世界里用上循环会非常伟大，它会加速学习的过程，这是个好主意。但话又说回来，有速度上限。

turns.en: The thing I keep coming back to is some version of this is amazing and I'm super in a sense AI-pilled in the sense of what I think these are things we're going to do and they're useful for, but I'm also cognizant of the idea that things bump up against the way I like to tell us to people as I said, look, you're really smart so you must understand being smart has limits.
turns.zh: 我反复想到的某种版本是：这一切很了不起，我在某种意义上非常上头（AI-pilled），认为这些是我们将会做、也确实有用的事；但我也清楚，事情会撞上天花板。我喜欢这样跟人讲：你这么聪明，所以你一定明白——聪明是有极限的。

turns.en: Being smart has limits and so the ability to just think your way to solutions is limited and so if you're going to build an automatic biology testing laboratory and you're going to connect it to a computer and the computer is going to come up with an idea and then it's going to run an experiment and it's going to iterate, that's awesome.
turns.zh: 聪明是有极限的，光靠想就能想到解决方案的能力是有限的。所以如果你要建一个自动化生物实验室，把它连上计算机，计算机提出一个点子，然后跑一个实验，再迭代——那太棒了。

turns.en: But if that experiment requires breeding mice and mice need a year to grow up and die, that experiment won't take time and it might be a great experiment, you might learn a lot and that's great, still going to take time and the lab is only so big and so you might have 5,000 great ideas, you're going to pick 20 and the model may be better.
turns.zh: 但如果那个实验需要繁育小鼠，而小鼠需要一年才能长大、死亡，那个实验就是需要花时间。它可能是个很棒的实验，你可能学到很多，那很好，但还是需要时间。实验室也只有那么大，你可能有 5000 个绝妙点子，你会挑 20 个，模型可能更会挑。

turns.en: The odds of that experiment might even be 1%. Turns out that might be 10 times better than the average researcher and that's amazing. It's still 1%.
turns.zh: 那个实验的成功率也许只有 1%。结果这也许是普通研究者的 10 倍好，那很了不起。但它仍然只是 1%。

turns.en: None of this is to be pessimistic, this is super amazing. Discovering all the things that we should know because it's already in our corpus that we forgot is awesome.
turns.zh: 说这些不是悲观，这一切超级棒。发现那些我们本该知道、却因为被遗忘而散落在语料里的东西——很了不起。

turns.en: Discovering all the things and better directing our research is awesome. Automating that research to move faster is awesome. We will learn that we'll push the frontier but this is not like suddenly the model looks around and says you guys missed it, here's some new world that you guys can't comprehend or what not.
turns.zh: 发现万物、更好地引导我们的研究——很了不起。让研究自动化以加速推进——很了不起。我们会学到很多、会推进前沿，但这不是那种模型突然环顾四周说'你们错过了这个，这里有个你们无法理解的新世界'的情况。

turns.en: I don't think that's where we're headed. It seems like the market has been, especially in private markets and the leading edge of investors thinking about AI, very focused on investing in supply-related stuff, like how are we going to build and serve all the intelligence versus what I'll call demand-related stuff, someone watching their personalized TV on their Meta app or whatever.
turns.zh: 我不认为我们要去那里。看起来市场——尤其在私募市场、以及思考 AI 的投资人最前端——一直非常专注于投资供给相关的东西：我们怎么建、怎么服务所有智能；而非我所说的需求相关的东西：有人用 Meta 应用看他们的个性化电视，之类。

turns.en: What do you think about that first batch of companies as investments? They're hard. I've joked I've been willfully ignorant about them and probably I'm sort of worse off for it but there's this big build-up and then you're trying to forecast inference demand.
turns.zh: 你觉得第一批那些公司作为投资怎么样？很难。我开玩笑说自己一直故意对它们保持无知，可能也因此错过了些什么。但有这么大的建设潮，然后你得预测推理需求。

turns.en: I can't forecast supply or demand within several orders of magnitude. This idea of how much more inference will people use as intelligence gets better and cheaper is a really, really hard thing and equally hard is how much better and cheaper inference is going to get and then even if you could somehow guess at those things then there's the whole value chain and you need to be at the bottleneck in order to capture
turns.zh: 我在供给或需求上都预测不到好几个数量级以内。'随着智能变得更好更便宜，人们会用多多少推理'这件事真的非常非常难；同样难的是推理会变得多好、多便宜；然后即便你有办法猜中这些，还有整条价值链，你得站在瓶颈环节才能捕获

turns.en: the rents and then of course finally you get to your actual competition with your competitors in that particular piece of the value chain. It's just a super hard thing as I think about my use of AI as a consumer, increasingly I'm doing stuff like instead of having the AI chatbot talk to my daughter or text with my daughter about how to do math, now I have it make a three blue one brown style video
turns.zh: 租金。最后当然还得面对你在该价值链环节上与竞争对手的真实竞争。这件事就是太难了。随着我作为消费者使用 AI，越来越多地，我在做这样的事：不再是让 AI 聊天机器人跟我女儿讲怎么做数学，而是让它做一个 Three Blue One Brown 风格的讲解视频，

turns.en: explainer so that she can see a nice 5 minute or 10 minute video on powers or area or circumference or something. It's super cool. I don't think I would do that if it was going to be $5 and so there's this thing where there's real price elasticity.
turns.zh: 让她可以看一个漂亮的 5 分钟、10 分钟视频，讲幂、面积或周长之类的。非常酷。如果这要花 5 美元，我想我是不会做的。所以这里存在真实的价格弹性。

turns.en: The point I'm trying to make is I'll film myself working out with my Muse app and it'll show me tip pointers on my form and I'll do that for very little money but I won't do that if the price point is real and I'm probably much less sensitive to the price than most people.
turns.zh: 我想说的点是：我会用我的 Muse 应用录自己健身，它会给我动作要领上的提示，花很少的钱我愿意做；但如果价格是实打实的，我就不会做了。而且我大概比大多数人对价格更不敏感。

turns.en: My demand is going to be really sensitive to the price which intrinsically I think does limit in some sense that the amount in total consumers are going to be willing to spend on this.
turns.zh: 我的需求对价格会非常敏感，这本质上我认为在某种意义上限制了消费者总体上愿意在这件事上花的钱。

turns.en: Maybe this is a time to talk about capital cycles or something. It sure does seem like the smartest people in the world and many or most of the best entrepreneurs in the world are heavily personally invested in this supply build out thing.
turns.zh: 也许这是聊聊资本周期（capital cycles）的时候。看起来世上最聪明的人、许多乃至最优秀的企业家，都在个人层面重度押注这场供给建设。

turns.en: If you watch SpaceX's investor day yesterday, this is basically the theme of it, arguably maybe the greatest entrepreneur of all time is dedicated to effectively doing this, building out the data center supply, etc.
turns.zh: 如果你看了昨天 SpaceX 的投资人日，这基本上就是主题。可以说，也许是史上最伟大的企业家，正致力于做这件事——建设数据中心供给，等等。

turns.en: This is just a historical question. If that's all true and there's so much uncertainty about supply and demand and there are other ways to go build businesses, products, make money, why do you think so many of the best entrepreneurs, the smartest people are so completely dedicating their lives to the build out of the supply?
turns.zh: 这是一个纯历史问题。如果这些都是真的，供给和需求又有那么多不确定性，还有别的路可走去建生意、做产品、赚钱，为什么你觉得那么多最优秀的企业家、最聪明的人，如此彻底地把人生献给供给侧的建设？

turns.en: This is a huge infrastructure build out of a huge and important technology and it would be impossible for there to be a huge infrastructure build out of a huge and important technology if there weren't a strong price signal and a ton of talent going at it.
turns.zh: 这是一场对巨大而重要技术的巨型基础设施大建设。如果没有强烈的价格信号和大量人才投入，这样的大建设根本不可能发生。

turns.en: So you may have your causality backwards. Obviously these things work both ways. Could you imagine a telling of the story where nobody interesting who'd made no money was building out the AI, right?
turns.zh: 所以你可能把因果搞反了。显然这两者是相互的。你能想象一个故事版本是：建 AI 的全是没赚过钱的、无趣的人吗？

turns.en: That's probably the best answer. And to be clear, this is a huge and important project. It's only happening because super smart and talented people are focusing their lives on it.
turns.zh: 那大概是最好的回答。要说清楚的是，这是一个宏大而重要的工程。它之所以在发生，正是因为超级聪明、有才华的人把人生聚焦于此。

turns.en: It's great that they are. They will have and deserve to make lots of money. It's just very, very hard from where I sit and there are probably people who are smarter and figured it out.
turns.zh: 他们这样做很好。他们会赚到、也理应赚到很多钱。只是以我所在的位置看，这件事非常非常难，也许有更聪明的人已经想明白了。

turns.en: From where I sit, it is very, very hard to figure out where one would invest along this and whether or not you'll get any money doing it. It's not to say that there isn't plenty of opportunity, I've just sort of decided to focus my attention more on the longer term equilibrium results that come from what the world goes to.
turns.zh: 以我所在的位置看，很难弄清楚该沿这条链条的哪里投资、以及做不做得成。这并不是说没有大量机会，只是我选择把注意力更多放在世界最终走向的长期均衡结果上。

turns.en: Instead of betting on which railroad tycoon is going to make money and how many railroads we need, I'm trying to think about, okay, once you have railroads, I'd love to have the foresight to figure out CPG brands come next.
turns.zh: 与其押注哪个铁路大亨会赚钱、我们需要多少条铁路，我更想的是：一旦有了铁路——我多希望自己有先见之明——接下来会是快消品牌（CPG brands）。

turns.en: That's the way I've been trying to think about it. Can you riff a little bit about what you've learned about capital cycles and innovation cycles like this?
turns.zh: 我一直试着这样思考。能不能展开讲讲你在这种资本周期与创新周期之中学到了什么？

turns.en: I would love your perspective on having studied so much market history. If we're in the middle of one of these, maybe the biggest one ever, what does history teach us about these cycles and how they work?
turns.zh: 你研究了那么多市场历史，很想听听你的视角：如果我们正处在其中一个大周期中段——也许是史上最大的一个——历史对这些周期的运作教会了我们什么？

turns.en: That's interesting to you. You could think about American society right now as a household that's saving money for a house. We're building a house and we're all kind of feeling pinched because all these resources are dedicated to building out this big AI infrastructure.
turns.zh: 这很有意思。你可以把当下的美国社会想象成一个为买房存钱的家庭。我们在盖一栋房子，大家都觉得手头有点紧，因为所有这些资源都被投入了这场 AI 大基建。

turns.en: All these electricians and plumbers and everything else are going to do these tasks and as consequence there's higher costs elsewhere in the economy and undoubtedly we're going to get a lot of value for it and we're going to keep pushing it because no one really knows.
turns.zh: 所有这些电工、水管工之类都在干这些活，其结果就是经济其他地方成本更高。毫无疑问我们从中会获得大量价值，而且我们会继续推进，因为没人真正知道。

turns.en: We're going to keep pushing it until eventually we overdo it and along the way people have to make tons of money because otherwise people won't keep pushing it.
turns.zh: 我们会一直推进，直到最终过头。而在这个过程中，人们必须赚到很多钱，否则没人会愿意继续推进。

turns.en: Because things have lead times and because it's a winner's curse, invariably the last person to stop will regret it and it's just so hard. It's just so hard and then you combine that with the fact that there's just so much dynamism in the technology here which I think was less true for other historic infrastructure buildouts.
turns.zh: 因为东西有建设周期，又因为是赢者诅咒，最后收手的那个人必然会后悔。这实在太难了，太难了。然后再叠加一层：这里的技术变化如此剧烈，我认为这比其他历史上的基建狂潮更甚。

turns.en: There's just so much change in terms of how you do these things. Other people have made the point, I don't think it's necessarily wrong that we talked about the models but even at the chips level or whatever, the potential for AI to commoditize even things like NVIDIA or...
turns.zh: 这些做法本身在剧烈变化。其他人也指出过——我认为未必错——我们谈的是模型，但即使在芯片层面也好，AI 甚至可能把 NVIDIA 这样的公司都商品化，鉴于 AI 到处自我改进……

turns.en: For cursive self-improvement everywhere at the... Everywhere and a lot of it ends up being just intelligence. NVIDIA quite literally makes flat files that they send to Taiwan.
turns.zh: 到处，而其中很多归结起来就只是智能。NVIDIA 卖的几乎就是字面意义上的平面文件（flat files），他们把这些文件发往台湾。

turns.en: Their flat files are very hard to make but what they have is a lot of people who think really hard about it and so in theory you could make them and also then the question becomes what if you step back a little from the frontier then the cost of making something comes way down.
turns.zh: 他们的平面文件很难做，但他们拥有的是一帮为此殚精竭虑的人，所以理论上别人也能做出来。然后问题就变成：如果你从前沿往后退一步，制造的成本就会大幅下降。

turns.en: In that world would your model be that physical and scale or the things that you'd want in a business that you were to back on the supply side of this equation, TSMC?
turns.zh: 在那种世界里，你的模型会是物理与规模吗？或者说，在这道方程的供给侧，你想押注的企业具备的要素——是 TSMC 吗？

turns.en: I don't want to carry myself around as some sort of TSMC expert. I mean certainly what they do has better attributes I think in that regard.
turns.zh: 我不想把自己当成 TSMC 专家到处晃悠。当然，从这方面看，他们做的事情具备的属性更好。

turns.en: They've also got this sort of interesting problem where they did this super hard thing that requires all this process power built over many years and it's super hard to replicate and much less amenable to AI just because it is so physical and because it's all these little things many of which aren't even legible to an AI.
turns.zh: 他们也面临一个有趣的问题：他们做了一件超难的事，需要多年积累起来的工艺能力，极难复制，而且对 AI 也远没那么容易被撼动——正因为它如此物理、如此多的小细节，其中许多对 AI 来说根本是不可辨识的。

turns.en: It's like some guy who is in the system kind of knows that you have to do this. Because there's so much demand and because they have millimedia they've basically caused every one in the world to seek to copy their moat.
turns.zh: 就像某个身在其中的人凭经验知道你必须这么做。因为需求太大、因为他们有产能，他们基本上促使世界上每个人都想办法复制他们的护城河。

turns.en: That's not a great fact but I think more generally stepping outside the AI build out if you think about businesses we talked about the meta example just the idea of businesses that have physical proximity or physical scale might benefit if they can use intelligence to serve their customers better or have lower cost than business accounts ones.
turns.zh: 这不是一个美妙的事实。但我认为更一般地，跳出 AI 建设本身来想企业——我们谈过 Meta 的例子——就是拥有物理邻近性或物理规模的企业，如果它们能用智能更好地服务客户、或成本更低，可能会受益。

turns.en: I want to go back through the natural compliments to intelligence just have you explain why it's a compliment to intelligence so then people can go away and think about OK what companies have this feature that might be interesting.
turns.zh: 我想回到智能的天然互补品这个话题：给人们解释一下为什么那是智能的互补品，这样大家就能去想——哦，什么样的公司有这个特征，可能值得关注。

turns.en: Good example to go talk about physical proximity. How would you think about DoorDash or Uber or these businesses that have local density effects that matter a lot.
turns.zh: 好的例子，聊聊物理邻近性。你会怎么思考 DoorDash 或 Uber 这类本地密度效应很重要的生意？

turns.en: Does intelligence being ubiquitous sort of naturally magnify all of the scale winners of this type where physical proximity is some sort of key advantage.
turns.zh: 智能无处不在，是否会天然放大所有这类规模赢家——那些以物理邻近性作为关键优势的公司？

turns.en: Well so if you're the low cost producer of something I'll give a sort of stylized example so if everyone has an AI agent then what happens is many decisions get offloaded the agent because the agent helps you optimize helps you pick up all the pennies and dollars and nickels and stuff that you were leading on the ground.
turns.zh: 嗯，如果你是某种东西的低成本生产者——我举个风格化的例子——如果人人都有一个 AI agent，那么发生的事情是：很多决策被交给 agent，因为 agent 帮你优化、帮你把你在地上漏掉的一分一毛全捡回来。

turns.en: So I think about consumer choices in a spectrum. On the one hand is maximizing my bank deposit. This is something where I think I can almost entirely defer to the AI's judgment as long as it's FDIC insured I just want the highest rate.
turns.zh: 所以我把消费者选择看成一条谱系。一端是最大化我的银行存款。这种事我觉得我几乎可以完全交给 AI 判断——只要是有 FDIC 保险的，我就要最高利率。

turns.en: On the other hand spend of the spectrum might be picking my favorite sweater. This is something where it's just all of my judgment the AI can source me things to look at but in the end I need to decide I can't really delegate that judgment to it.
turns.zh: 另一端，比如挑我最喜欢的毛衣。这种事全凭我的判断，AI 可以帮我找来一堆可看的东西，但最终我得自己定，我没法把这种判断委托出去。

turns.en: And there's a spectrum and so let's just pretend for a moment that garbage collection is something where I can defer the judgment. You might say no I really care about the guy and I trust the service and there's driving to my house or whatever but let's just settle aside for a second.
turns.zh: 中间是一条谱系。我们姑且假设垃圾清运是我可以外包判断的事。你可能会说：不，我真的很在意那个人、我信任这个服务、他还开到我家门口之类的，但我们先放下这些。

turns.en: So right now if I'm in the waste collection business I might be great at it but it's still really hard to get people to bother to switch. I doubt you know what you pay for garbage collection off the top of your head.
turns.zh: 所以眼下，如果我做垃圾清运生意，我可能做得很好，但要让人们费心去切换仍然非常难。我打赌你随口说不出垃圾清运要花多少钱。

turns.en: Many people do but I doubt you do. And so what happens is you have to do all this work to get people to pay attention to bother to switch garbage collections companies even if you're offering a better service at a lower price.
turns.zh: 很多人知道，但我打赌你不知道。所以发生的是，你必须费很大劲才能让人们去关注、去费心切换垃圾清运公司——即便你提供的是更好、更便宜的服务。
